title: Perfect Number
statement:
Call a positive integer **perfect** when adding up all of its positive divisors other than the number itself gives back the number. Here a divisor of `x` is any integer that divides `x` with no remainder.

Given the integer `num`, return `true` when `num` is perfect and `false` otherwise.
notes:
## Intuition

Divisors come in pairs: if `divisor` divides `num`, so does `num / divisor`, and one of the two is at most √`num`. So instead of testing every number up to `num / 2` (the brute force, up to 5·10⁷ checks), walk `divisor` only up to √`num` and add both members of each pair. That is at most 10⁴ steps for the largest input.

## Approach

1. `1` has no proper divisors at all, so it is not perfect.
2. Every other `num` is divisible by `1`, so start `sum` at `1` (and never add `num` itself, the partner of `1`).
3. For each `divisor` from `2` while `divisor * divisor <= num`: when it divides `num`, add it and its `partner = num / divisor`.
4. If `partner` equals `divisor` (a perfect square), add it only once.
5. `num` is perfect exactly when `sum === num`.

## Example 1, step by step

`num = 28`, `sum = 1`. `divisor = 2` divides 28 with `partner = 14`, so `sum = 17`. `3` does not divide 28. `divisor = 4` gives `partner = 7`, so `sum = 28`. `5 * 5 = 25 <= 28` but 5 does not divide 28; `6 * 6 = 36 > 28` ends the loop. `sum === 28`, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(√num): one modulo test per candidate up to the square root.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- `num = 1` would give `sum = 1` and wrongly return `true` without the early check.
- Adding the square root twice for square numbers (`16`, `10^8`) overcounts.
- Do not include `num` itself, which is why the loop starts at `2` instead of pairing `1` with `num`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sum` | total of the proper divisors found so far |
| `divisor` | candidate small divisor, up to √`num` |
| `partner` | the matching large divisor `num / divisor` |

narration.2: 1 has no divisors besides itself, so it cannot be perfect.
narration.5: 1 divides every number, so it starts the sum; its partner is num itself, which is excluded.
narration.6: Only try small divisors up to the square root; each one reveals a partner.
narration.7: Does this candidate divide num exactly?
narration.9: Its partner num / divisor is also a divisor.
narration.10: For a perfect square the two are equal...
narration.11: ...so the partner is added only when it is different.
narration.15: num is perfect exactly when its proper divisors add up to it.
